Find Q3: median of upper half above Q2
Draw box Q1 to Q3 with median line, whiskers to min/max
lessons.tip: The IQR is the best measure of spread when outliers exist, because it ignores extreme values and focuses on the middle 50%.

quiz.q: IQR=12, Q3=50. Upper outlier bound?
Median closer to Q1 means:
quiz.explanation: More data in lower half, tail extends right.

lessons.title: Scatter Plots & Lines of Best Fit
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of scatter plots & lines of best fit
lessons.formula:
Line of Best Fit (slope-intercept):
  y = mx + b

Slope formula (using two points on the line):
  m = (y₂ – y₁) / (x₂ – x₁)
lessons.content:
A scatter plot displays pairs of numerical data as points on a coordinate plane. Each point represents one observation, with the x-value for one variable and the y-value for the other. By looking at the overall pattern of points, you can determine whether two variables are related and how strongly.

When points rise from left to right, the variables have positive correlation; when they fall, they have negative correlation. An outlier is a point that sits far away from the general trend and may need special attention. The line of best fit (or trend line) is a straight line drawn as close as possible to all the data points, modeling the overall relationship.

To draw a line of best fit by eye, place a ruler so that roughly half the points fall above and half below the line. Once the line is drawn, pick two convenient points on it to calculate its slope (m) and y-intercept (b), giving you the equation y = mx + b you can use to make predictions.
steps: Plot every data pair (x, y) as a point on the coordinate plane.
Examine the overall pattern — positive, negative, or no correlation.
Draw a straight trend line that passes as close to all points as possible.
Pick two points on the trend line and calculate slope: m = (y₂ – y₁) / (x₂ – x₁).
Use slope m and one point to solve for b (y-intercept), then write y = mx + b.

examples.title: Finding the Line of Best Fit
examples.text: A scatter plot shows study hours (x) and test scores (y): (1, 60), (2, 68), (3, 75), (4, 78), (5, 85), (6, 90). Drawing a trend line through (1, 62) and (5, 86): m = (86 – 62)/(5 – 1) = 24/4 = 6. Using (1, 62): 62 = 6(1) + b → b = 56. Line: y = 6x + 56.

examples.title: Making a Prediction
examples.text: Using y = 6x + 56, predict the test score for a student who studies 7 hours: y = 6(7) + 56 = 42 + 56 = 98. The model predicts a score of 98.

lessons.tip: When drawing a line of best fit by eye, do NOT connect the first and last points unless they truly represent the trend. Think of it as splitting the difference so about half the points are above and half are below.

quiz.q: If points on a scatter plot generally go from lower-left to upper-right, what type of correlation is shown?
quiz.explanation: Points rising from left to right indicate that as x increases, y also increases — this is positive correlation.

quiz.q: A line of best fit has the equation y = 2x + 5. What is the slope?
quiz.explanation: In y = mx + b, m is the slope. Here m = 2.

quiz.q: An outlier in a scatter plot is best described as:
options: The point closest to the origin
A data point that lies far from the overall trend
The point with the largest x-value
The average of all data points
quiz.explanation: An outlier is a point that does not follow the general pattern of the data and sits noticeably far from the trend line.

quiz.q: Using y = 3x + 10, what is the predicted y-value when x = 4?

lessons.title: Sampling Methods & Populations
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of sampling methods & populations
lessons.formula:
Sample proportion:
  p̂ = (number with trait) / n

Sample mean:
  x̄ = (sum of all values) / n

Margin of error (conceptual):
  estimate ± margin of error
lessons.content:
In statistics, a population is the entire group you want to learn about, while a sample is the smaller group you actually study. Because surveying everyone in a population is usually too expensive or impractical, we rely on well-chosen samples to draw conclusions about the whole group.

A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected, which prevents bias. Common random methods include simple random sampling (pulling names from a hat), systematic sampling (every k-th person on a list), and stratified sampling (dividing the population into subgroups first, then sampling within each subgroup). A biased sample systematically favors certain outcomes — for example, surveying only people at a gym about exercise habits.

The key question to ask about any sample is: Is this sample representative of the population? If the sample reflects the population's diversity and characteristics, you can trust the results. If not, the conclusions may be misleading, no matter how many people were surveyed.
steps: Define the population you want to study (who or what?).
Choose a sampling method: simple random, systematic, or stratified.
Determine an appropriate sample size — larger samples give more reliable results.
Collect data from the selected sample members.
Analyze sample results and use them to make inferences about the population.

examples.title: Simple Random Sample
examples.text: A school has 500 students and wants to survey 50 about their favorite lunch. Assign each student a number 1–500, then use a random number generator to pick 50 numbers. Every student had an equal chance, so this is a simple random sample.

examples.title: Identifying a Biased Sample
examples.text: A researcher surveys people leaving a movie theater about how often they watch movies. This is a convenience sample and is biased because people at a theater likely watch movies more often than the general public. A better method would be a random phone survey of town residents.

lessons.tip: Whenever you read a statistic in the news, ask: 'How was the sample chosen?' If the article doesn't mention the sampling method, the results may be unreliable.

quiz.q: A sampling method where every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected is called a:
quiz.explanation: A random sample ensures every member of the population has an equal chance of selection, which minimizes bias.

quiz.q: Surveying only people at a health-food store about their diet is an example of:
quiz.explanation: This survey only reaches people already shopping at a health-food store, so it systematically over-represents health-conscious individuals — that's bias.

quiz.q: In stratified sampling, the population is first divided into:
quiz.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) based on a characteristic (e.g., grade level), then samples from each stratum.

quiz.q: Why do researchers usually study a sample instead of an entire population?
options: A sample is always more accurate
It is usually faster, cheaper, and more practical
Populations are too small to measure
quiz.explanation: Studying every member of a population is often impractical due to time, cost, and access. A well-chosen sample provides reliable estimates about the whole population.

lessons.title: Theoretical vs Experimental Probability
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of theoretical vs experimental probability
lessons.formula:
Theoretical Probability:
  P(event) = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes)

Experimental Probability:
  P(event) = (times event occurred) / (total trials)

Complement Rule:
  P(not A) = 1 – P(A)
lessons.content:
Theoretical probability is what you expect to happen based on reasoning — it's the ratio of favorable outcomes to total equally-likely outcomes. For example, when you flip a fair coin, P(heads) = 1/2 because there are 2 outcomes and 1 is favorable. Theoretical probability assumes perfect conditions.

Experimental probability is what actually happens when you perform an experiment or run a simulation. If you flip a coin 100 times and get 47 heads, the experimental probability is 47/100 = 0.47. As the number of trials increases, experimental probability usually gets closer to theoretical probability — a principle known as the Law of Large Numbers.

Both types are useful. Theoretical probability helps you predict outcomes before an experiment, while experimental probability tells you what is actually happening in real trials. When they differ significantly, it may indicate the experiment isn't random or the sample size is too small.
steps: Identify the sample space — list all possible outcomes.
Count the total number of equally-likely outcomes.
Count the number of favorable outcomes (those matching the event).
Calculate theoretical probability: P = favorable / total.
If running an experiment, calculate experimental probability: P = occurred / trials, and compare.

examples.title: Rolling a Die
examples.text: What is the theoretical probability of rolling a number greater than 4 on a fair six-sided die? The sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Favorable outcomes: {5, 6}, so 2 out of 6. P = 2/6 = 1/3 ≈ 0.333. If you roll the die 60 times and get 22 rolls greater than 4, experimental P = 22/60 ≈ 0.367 — close to the theoretical value.

examples.title: Spinning a Spinner
examples.text: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 3 red, 2 blue, 2 green, 1 yellow. P(red) = 3/8 = 0.375 (theoretical). You spin 40 times and land on red 14 times. Experimental P(red) = 14/40 = 0.35. The values are reasonably close.

lessons.tip: As a quick check, probabilities must always be between 0 and 1 (inclusive). If your answer is negative or greater than 1, double-check your counting of favorable and total outcomes.

quiz.q: A fair coin is flipped once. What is the theoretical probability of getting tails?
quiz.explanation: There are 2 equally-likely outcomes (heads, tails) and 1 favorable (tails). P = 1/2.

quiz.q: You flip a coin 50 times and get heads 28 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
quiz.explanation: Experimental probability = times occurred / total trials = 28/50 = 0.56.

quiz.q: A bag has 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles. What is the theoretical probability of drawing a red marble?
According to the Law of Large Numbers, as you increase the number of trials:
options: Experimental probability gets further from theoretical
Experimental probability gets closer to theoretical
quiz.explanation: The Law of Large Numbers states that with more trials, experimental results tend to converge on the theoretical probability.

lessons.title: Probability of Compound Events
lessons.description: Calculate probabilities of compound events using tree diagrams, organized lists, and the multiplication rule.
lessons.formula:
Probability of a compound event:
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)  [Independent events]
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A)  [Dependent events]

Example (independent):
P(coin heads, then die 6)
= (1/2) × (1/6) = 1/12
lessons.content:
A compound event is an event that involves two or more simple events happening together or in sequence. For example, flipping a coin and then rolling a die is a compound event. To find the probability of a compound event, you need to understand the sample space — the complete list of all possible outcomes. For the coin-and-die example, there are 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely outcomes. Organizing these outcomes systematically is the key to accurate probability calculations.

Tree diagrams are visual tools that map out all possible outcomes of a compound event. Each branch represents one possibility, and following the branches from left to right traces a complete outcome path. When events are independent (the outcome of one does not affect the other), you can use the multiplication rule: multiply the probabilities along each branch. For example, the probability of flipping heads and then rolling a 3 is (1/2) × (1/6) = 1/12. When events are dependent, the probability of the second event changes based on the first. Drawing cards without replacement is a classic example: after drawing one king from a deck, the probability of drawing a second king is now 3/51 instead of 4/52.

Compound probability appears everywhere in daily life. Weather forecasts combine the probability of rain with wind conditions. Games of chance involve drawing cards, rolling dice, or spinning wheels in sequence. In quality control, the probability that two independent inspections both pass a product helps determine defect rates. Organized lists and tree diagrams help ensure you count every outcome exactly once, avoiding both overcounting and undercounting. As you progress, you will connect these ideas to permutations, combinations, and statistical inference. Building a strong intuition for compound probability now provides the reasoning skills needed for data science, risk assessment, and informed decision making in an uncertain world.
steps: Identify whether the events are independent (one outcome does not affect the other) or dependent.
List or diagram the sample space using a tree diagram, table, or organized list.
Find the probability of the first event.
Find the probability of the second event (use the conditional probability if the events are dependent).
Multiply the probabilities using P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent or P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A) for dependent events.

examples.title: Independent Events: Spinner and Coin
examples.text: A spinner has 4 equal sections (red, blue, green, yellow). You spin and flip a coin. P(red AND heads) = P(red) × P(heads) = (1/4) × (1/2) = 1/8. There are 8 total outcomes in the sample space, and red-heads is one of them.

examples.title: Dependent Events: Drawing Marbles
examples.text: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. You draw one, keep it, then draw another. P(both red) = P(red first) × P(red second | red first) = (5/8) × (4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14. After removing one red marble, only 4 red remain out of 7 total.

lessons.tip: Always ask yourself: does the first event change the probabilities for the second event? If yes, the events are dependent and you must adjust the second probability. If no, they are independent and you can simply multiply.

quiz.q: A coin is flipped twice. What is the probability of getting heads both times?
A bag has 6 red and 4 green marbles. One is drawn and NOT replaced, then another is drawn. What is the probability both are green?
quiz.explanation: P(green first) = 4/10. P(green second | green first) = 3/9. P(both) = (4/10) × (3/9) = 12/90 = 2/15.

quiz.q: You roll a die and flip a coin. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
quiz.explanation: 6 die outcomes × 2 coin outcomes = 12 total outcomes.

quiz.q: A standard deck has 52 cards. Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are aces?
quiz.explanation: P(ace first) = 4/52. P(ace second | ace first) = 3/51. P(both) = (4/52) × (3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221.
